newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya president to meet opposition on reforms.
newsitem.headline: Kenya president to meet opposition on reforms.

text.p: Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi agreed on Wednesday to meet opposition leaders next week, stepping up dialogue in the face of protests by groups demanding constitutional reforms.

But leaders of an opposition-backed campaign for reforms said Moi's talks with the leader of the opposition in parliament on Wednesday and religious leaders on Tuesday were not enough to prompt them to abandon their plans to pressure the president.
Michael Wamalwa, opposition leader in parliament, said Moi in 10 minutes of "cordial" talks with him on Wednesday agreed to a meeting between the government and opposition leaders next week.

"The president acceded to my request for a meeting between the government and a team of opposition leaders next week. I have immediately initiated consultations with my colleagues in the opposition towards this end," he told a news conference.

"We are not asking for a whole lot. We are asking for minimum reforms that will level the playing field so we can go into free and fair elections," he said. "The president seemed to be in the mood for dialogue."

Wamalwa leads the FORD-Kenya party but is not himself on the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC), an alliance of opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies demanding constitutional reforms before a general election.
Opposition politician Richard Leakey, an NCEC member, told Reuters the dialogue opened by Moi on Monday would not prompt the committee to tone down its campaign to press for reforms.
"The NCEC is very broad-based. Mr Wamalwa has no mandate to negotiate on behalf of other people," said Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party and Kenya's former wildlife guardian.
"Of course I am delighted to see Moi having dialogue but we have an agenda, we have set conditions, we have laid it all out and want nothing less," said Leakey, a famous palaeontologist.
Leakey said on Tuesday the NCEC had identified the Indian Ocean city of Mombasa, the centre of Kenya's tourism industry, as its next focus and hoped for an agreement with Moi by the end of July.

In his first major conciliatory move, Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years, met 17 Christian and Moslem religious leaders on Tuesday and agreed the need for a review of the constitution. No date was set for the review.
The NCEC demands what it calls "minimal" reforms before a general election this year. No date for the presidential and parliamentary polls has been set. The reforms would reduce Moi's power.

Reverend Timothy Njoya, a Presbyterian cleric and an NCEC member, dismissed Moi's meeting with religious leaders and said it would not sidetrack the reform drive, which has led to bloody clashes between police and protesters in Kenya since June.

"If NCEC representatives had gone it would mean something. But Moi is ignoring all that and appointing his own reformists and making himself appear a reformer. That is not dialogue," said Njoya, whose arm was broken by police during July 7 clashes in Nairobi between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators.
"These people are going to dilute the reform process. Their agreement to review the constitution is a move in the right direction but we will call for more action," Njoya added.
At least nine people were killed in Kenya on July 7 during the country's worst political violence in seven years when riot police broke up a day of demonstrations called by the NCEC.
The July 7 violence, which closed down Nairobi, was followed by student unrest in the capital last week, leading to closure of two universities followed by Kenya Polytechnic on Monday.
